chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan, from his two brothers Muhammad and Ahmad, from their father, from Dawud ibn Abi Yazid, from Burayd ibn Mu'awiya, who said:

A man died and left me in his will, along with another man, or two men. One of them said, 'Take half of what he left and give me the half of what he left.' The other refused him. They asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, and he said, 'That is for him.' This refers to the one who refused the other's claim to exclusive possession of half the estate.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Babawayh (may God have mercy on him) mentioned that this report, he does not act upon it nor issue fatwa based on it, but he acts upon the first report, assuming that the two are contradictory. However, the matter is not as he assumed, because the Imam's (peace be upon him) statement 'That is for him' does not explicitly mean that it is for the claimant who sought exclusive possession of half the estate. It is not impossible that what is meant by his statement 'That is for him' is the one who refused to submit to his partner's desire, so the conclusion of the speech is that he has the right to refuse him and not respond to his request. On this basis, there is no contradiction between them in any case.
ai.seo_question: How do Shia jurists interpret the Imam's ruling 'That is for him' regarding two executors disputing the estate?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the Imam’s ruling 'That is for him' is interpreted by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Babawayh (al-Kulayni) not as granting exclusive ownership to the claimant, but as affirming the right of the refusing executor to withhold consent, thereby resolving the apparent contradiction with other reports. This highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling seemingly conflicting hadiths through contextual interpretation (ta'wil) rather than dismissal, emphasizing the autonomy of executors in managing the estate.
